newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives impossible to lead - Clarke.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives impossible to lead - Clarke.

text.p: Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke on Thursday rounded on dissident ruling Conservatives, saying they made it impossible for Prime Minister John Major to lead the party.
"John can lead a party, but there are sometimes parties that are simply not capable of being led," Clarke said in a BBC radio interview in which his frustration with internal bickering was plain.
Clarke spoke after smouldering right wing discontent burst into the open with a vicious attack on Major by one legislator.
The member of parliament, writing anonymously in the left-wing Tribune weekly under the pen name Cassandra, accused Major of failing to stand up for Britain in the European Union.
"More and more Tory MPs are waking up to the fact that John Major is terminally inadequate at defending Britain's interests and leading our party," the MP said.
"I've never heard a more preposterous remark in my life," Clarke told BBC interviewer Jimmy Young.

"If the backbenches of the Conservative Party would only come to their senses and stop writing rubbish like that in Tribune, we could beat this inadequate Labour Party completely out of sight," he said.
The opposition Labour Party is currently some 20 points ahead of the Conservatives in the opinion polls with a general election due by May 22.

Clarke, who on Tuesday delivered an annual budget designed to consolidate the healthy growth which the British economy is currently enjoying, said but for internal strife the Conservatives should be coasting to another election victory.

"If you look at the present state of the economy and how Britain's doing, John Major should be on to a walk-over at the next election. I cannot believe that we've got ourselves behind in the polls," he said.

His words were seen as a big embarrassment for the Conservatives. Labour's economic spokesman Gordon Brown gleefully described them as "an astonishing attack on his own party, an admission of factional in-fighting".
Clarke is the most pro-European member of Major's cabinet.

His stance towards Brussels has made him deeply unpopular with the "Eurosceptic" wing of the party who believe only his opposition has stopped Major from ruling out taking Britain into an EU single currency in the next parliament.
However, Clarke said he was "not mad set" on Britain abandoning the pound sterling.
On Monday, Clarke interrupted preparations for his budget to repulse an attack on the government by the "Eurosceptics".

They were angry at the government's refusal to hold a full parliamentary debate on European Union documents on preparation for a single currency -- a move which they see as entailing an unacceptable loss of British sovereignty.
Clarke told parliament the documents would not bind Britain to a single currency and nothing would be approved without parliament's authorisation.
